docs.title: list-cameras
docs.text:
Enumerate connected FLIR cameras and print their index and serial number.

msw-flir list-cameras --driver flycap
msw-flir list-cameras --driver spinnaker

Requires the FlyCapture2 SDK (PyCapture2) or Spinnaker SDK (PySpin) Python wrapper to be installed. These are Windows-only native libraries.

Example output: 

FlyCapture2: 2 camera(s) found
  [0]  serial=12345678  model=Chameleon3 CM3-U3-13Y3M
  [1]  serial=87654321  model=Chameleon3 CM3-U3-13Y3M

The index shown is the value to pass as cameras.cam_index or --cam-index.

docs.title: probe-cameras
docs.text:
Print the index and serial of each connected camera without opening it, so a setup can name its cameras by serial instead of by enumeration index.

msw-flir probe-cameras --driver flycap
msw-flir probe-cameras --driver spinnaker --json
Option Default Description --driver, -d flycap flycap or spinnaker --json off Print {driver, source, count, cameras: [{index, serial}], error} --timeout 10 Seconds before the SDK probe is killed

source says where the answer came from:

  • sdk: the FlyCapture2 or Spinnaker C library (FlyCapture2_C.dll, SpinnakerC_v140.dll), loaded through ctypes in a child process. No Python SDK wrapper is needed. Index and serial per camera.
  • usb: the SDK was missing, crashed or hung. Windows PnP devices from vendor 0x1E10: count and serials, no index order. Only the parent "USB Composite Device" (USB\VID_1E10&PID_xxxx\<serial>) counts; its serial is hex and is reported in decimal, like the SDK (hex 00BC614E is serial 12345678).
  • none: neither worked; exits 1.

The C library is searched in MSW_FLIR_FC2_DLL / MSW_FLIR_SPIN_DLL (full path), then on the DLL search path, then in the default Program Files install directories.

Spinnaker probe untested

The FlyCapture2 probe is checked on Flea3 USB3 cameras. The Spinnaker probe (DLL names, install folders, function calls) has not run on hardware yet.

docs.title: Naming cameras by serial
docs.text:
Add serial to each camera in the setup YAML (msw-core CameraUnit):

cameras:
  backend: flir_bonsai
  driver: flycap
  cameras:
    - {index: 0, name: top, serial: "12345678"}
    - {index: 1, name: side, serial: "87654321"}

Before Bonsai starts, resolve_camera_units checks the probe against the setup. FlyCapture launches each camera at the index the SDK reports for its serial; Spinnaker passes the serial to Bonsai (cam1serial). A serial that is not connected, or fewer cameras than the setup needs, refuses the start. With no serials configured only the count is checked. With source none it warns and launches by configured index. With source usb serials are checked too, but FlyCapture keeps the configured index.

A camera has started when its first frame is in <cam_basename>.avi (the file has data, about 5 s after launch). The other signals mislead: Bonsai's return code is 0 when it finds no camera (it exits about 4 to 5 s after launch), and the timestamps CSV stays 0 B until its first 4 KB block, several seconds of frames. The start fails (BonsaiStartError) when Bonsai exits before the first frame, at any time, or when start_timeout (15 s) passes without one; Bonsai is then stopped. After an exit without a frame the camera can still be held for a few seconds, so Bonsai is relaunched once after 3 s (retry_delay), unless the caller passes expect_present=False because the probe did not see the camera. MultiCameraRunner.start waits for all cameras against one deadline and stops them all if one fails.

docs.title: Verifying on a rig
docs.text:
1. msw flir probe-cameras -d flycap (and -d spinnaker): source should be sdk and the serials should match the camera labels.
  2. Unplug one camera and run it again: the count drops and the remaining serial keeps its identity even when its index changes.
  3. List the USB devices with Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | ? InstanceId -like 'USB\VID_1E10*' in PowerShell: the entry without MI_ ends in the hex serial.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Launch N independent Bonsai camera subprocesses (one per camera index).

msw-flir run <output_dir> <session> [options]

Arguments:

Argument Description output_dir Root directory where video output is written session Session base name used for folder and file naming

Options:

Option Default Description --n-cameras, -n 1 Number of camera subprocesses to launch --driver, -d flycap Camera driver: flycap or spinnaker --fps 60 Target frame rate (FlyCapture only; ignored for Spinnaker) --bonsai-exe $BONSAI_EXE Path to Bonsai.exe --workflow auto Override the workflow stem name

Each camera uses the 1-cam Bonsai workflow with its own cam_index. Press Ctrl+C to stop all cameras cleanly.

Example:

msw-flir run D:\DATA\video mouse001__20260524 --n-cameras 2 --fps 60

docs.title: test-record
docs.text:
Run a short test recording from a single camera to verify the setup. The duration counts from the first frame. Bonsai exits 0 even when it could not record, so the command judges the outcome itself: it exits 1 when no frame arrives, when Bonsai exited before the stop was requested (at any time), or when <session>.timestamps.csv is missing or empty.

msw-flir test-record [options]

Options:

Option Default Description --output-dir ~/msw_flir_test Output directory --session test Session name --cam-index, -c 0 Camera index --driver, -d flycap Camera driver --fps 30 Frame rate --duration 5.0 Recording duration in seconds --bonsai-exe $BONSAI_EXE, then the find-bonsai locations Path to Bonsai.exe --workflow auto Override workflow stem name

Example:

msw-flir test-record --cam-index 1 --driver spinnaker --duration 10

docs.title: Single camera
docs.text:
from msw_flir_bonsai.runner import BonsaiCameraRunner

runner = BonsaiCameraRunner(
    workflow="run-flir-flycap-1cam",
    output_dir=r"D:\DATA\video",
    session="mouse001__20260524",
    cam_index=0,
    fps=60,
    driver="flycap",
    bonsai_exe=r"C:\Users\lab\AppData\Local\Bonsai\Bonsai.exe",
)

runner.start()
# ... behavioural task runs ...
runner.stop()
runner.wait(timeout=15)

bonsai_exe falls back to the BONSAI_EXE environment variable if not provided.

docs.title: Multiple cameras (one process per camera)
docs.text:
from msw_flir_bonsai.runner import MultiCameraRunner

multi = MultiCameraRunner.from_config(
    n_cameras=2,
    driver="flycap",
    output_dir=r"D:\DATA\video",
    session="mouse001__20260524",
    fps=60,
    bonsai_exe=r"C:\...\Bonsai.exe",
)

multi.start()
# ... task runs ...
multi.stop()

from_config always uses the 1-cam workflow and spawns N independent processes with consecutive cam_index values (0, 1, …). A crash in one process does not affect the others.

docs.title: MSW integration (via CameraClient protocol)
docs.text:
When used through murineshiftwork, the runner is wrapped by FlirBonsaiClient and called via the four-method CameraClient protocol:

from murineshiftwork.hardware.camera.client import make_camera_client

cameras_config = setup_config.cameras  # CameraConfig from setup YAML
client = make_camera_client(cameras_config)

if client:
    client.preflight()           # checks bonsai_exe path
    client.start_recording(output_path, session_name)
    # ... task ...
    client.stop_recording()
    client.teardown()

See the murineshiftwork setup config docs for the full YAML reference.

docs.title: Preprocessing camera timestamps
docs.text:
Bonsai writes a headerless CSV per camera with three columns, in this order:

Column FlyCapture Spinnaker gpio_state embeddedGPIOPinState ExposureEndLineStatusAll timestamp_raw embeddedTimeStamp (packed cycle timer) Timestamp (ns) frame_counter embeddedFrameCounter FrameID

preprocess_camera_csv decodes timestamp_raw per driver into timestamp_s. FlyCapture packs seconds mod 128 (bits 31-25), 8 kHz cycles (bits 24-12) and 1/3072 cycle offsets (bits 11-0); the 128 s rollover is unwrapped. Spinnaker nanoseconds are divided by 1e9.

from msw_flir_bonsai.timestamps import preprocess_camera_csv

df = preprocess_camera_csv(
    "cam0.timestamps.csv",
    driver="flycap",        # or "spinnaker"
    session_start_s=None,   # or a Bpod event time to zero the clock
)
# df columns: frame_index, gpio_state, timestamp_raw, frame_counter, timestamp_s

gpio_state is the bitmask of all camera lines. Read one line with line_state(df["gpio_state"], bit); the FlyCapture barcode input is bit 31.

docs.title: Detect dropped frames
docs.text:
from msw_flir_bonsai.timestamps import detect_dropped_frames

dropped = detect_dropped_frames(df, expected_fps=60.0)
n_dropped = dropped.sum()
print(f"{n_dropped} dropped frames")

docs.title: Aligning camera timestamps to Bpod
docs.text: Both functions read one line of gpio_state, chosen by line_bit (default 31, the FlyCapture barcode input). The Spinnaker line bit depends on the wiring: confirm it on a recording and pass it explicitly.

docs.title: Barcode alignment
docs.text:
The camera must decode with the settings Bpod sent the barcodes with (the session's barcodes:, or the task's barcode settings). Bits need about three frames: 100 ms bits for a 60 fps camera. Shorter bits are refused with a warning.

from ttl_barcoder import BarcodeConfig
from msw_flir_bonsai.alignment import extract_camera_barcodes, align_barcodes

config = BarcodeConfig(bit_duration_ms=100, init_duration_ms=100)
cam_barcodes = extract_camera_barcodes(df, config, line_bit=31)
# bpod_barcodes: list of (time_s, barcode_int) from Bpod BNC events
offset_s = align_barcodes(bpod_barcodes, cam_barcodes, max_hamming=2)

df["bpod_time"] = df["timestamp_s"] + offset_s

docs.title: TTL-edge alignment (fallback)
docs.text:
from msw_flir_bonsai.alignment import align_ttl_edges

# bpod_trial_times: list of trial-start times in Bpod clock
offset_s = align_ttl_edges(df, bpod_trial_times, line_bit=31)
df["bpod_time"] = df["timestamp_s"] + offset_s

docs.title: Bundled workflows
docs.text:
Four Bonsai workflow XMLs are shipped as package data and located at runtime via msw_flir_bonsai.bonsai_workflows.workflow_path(name).

Stem name Driver Cameras run-flir-flycap-1cam FlyCapture2 1 run-flir-spinnaker-1cam Spinnaker 1 run-flir-flycap-2cam FlyCapture2 2 (legacy single-process) run-flir-spinnaker-2cam Spinnaker 2 (legacy single-process)

The 1-cam workflows are the standard path. MultiCameraRunner.from_config always selects the 1-cam variant and launches N independent subprocesses: one per camera index. The 2-cam workflows are retained for reference but are not used by the Python runner.

docs.title: External properties (Bonsai CLI -p flags)
docs.text:
Each 1-cam workflow exposes these properties, settable via Bonsai.exe --start -p key=value:

Property Type Workflows Description basepath string all Root output directory session string all Session base name cam1idx int all Camera index (0-based) cam1serial string spinnaker only (1cam) Camera serial; when set, SpinnakerCapture selects by SerialNumber and ignores cam1idx cam1fps int flycap only Target frame rate: sets FramesPerSecond on the FlyCapture node cam1ts bool flycap only Enable embedded timestamp cam1framecounter bool flycap only Enable frame counter

Spinnaker frame rate

The Spinnaker workflow has no cam1fps externalized property: the frame rate is not settable via CLI -p. Set it directly in the Bonsai workflow XML (open in the Bonsai editor, find the SpinnakerCapture node, set AcquisitionFrameRate).

The BonsaiCameraRunner._build_cmd() method assembles these into the subprocess command automatically.

docs.title: Control model
docs.text:
Bonsai is launched with --start --no-editor so the workflow begins immediately without user interaction:

Bonsai.exe workflow.bonsai --start --no-editor -p basepath="D:\..." -p session="..." ...
  • Start: the --start flag; no keyboard or socket needed.
  • Stop: stop() creates a stop file whose path is passed to Bonsai in MSW_BONSAI_STOP_FILE. Extensions\key-ctrl-stop.bonsai checks for it every 0.2 s (and for the caller's process, MSW_BONSAI_PARENT_PID, having exited) and then completes the stream, so the video and CSV writers flush and close and Bonsai exits on its own. If that does not happen within the timeout, the process is killed; on Windows the whole process tree (taskkill /T), because Bonsai.exe relaunches itself as a child worker.
  • Bonsai runs in its own process group, so a Ctrl+C in the calling console does not reach it before the caller has shut down and requested the stop.

docs.title: Bundled extension workflows
docs.text:
Every bundled workflow includes three extension workflows from Extensions\, shipped with the package:

file role key-ctrl-stop.bonsai completes the stream on the stop file (see above) key-ctrl-start.bonsai pass-through: start is handled by --start measure-rate.bonsai pass-through: no rate display in --no-editor mode

docs.title: Live preview
docs.text: If a workflow has a <workflow>.bonsai.layout next to it (bundled for run-flir-flycap-1cam), each camera starts with --visualizer-layout pointing at its own copy of that layout, with the preview window shifted right by camera index so several cameras sit side by side. The copy is deleted on stop().

docs.title: Alternative control mechanisms
docs.text:
If per-trial start/stop (without relaunching Bonsai) is ever needed:

Mechanism Notes TCP NetworkCommand Add a NetworkCommand source to the workflow; Python sends a string over TCP to trigger transitions File-system sentinel Bonsai FileSystemWatcher watches for a file; Python creates/deletes it OSC Low-latency via Bonsai OSC package; common in neuroscience tooling

For the standard MSW use case (one Bonsai process per session), --start plus the stop file is sufficient.

docs.title: Output structure
docs.text:
The IronPython transform inside the workflow creates:

<basepath>/
  <session>/
    <session>__<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>/
      <session>__<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>__cam0.avi   # video
      <session>__<YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS>__cam0.csv   # metadata (gpio, timestamp, counter)

The preprocess_camera_csv function loads and cleans the CSV; see Python API for details.

docs.title: Locating bundled workflows
docs.text:
from msw_flir_bonsai.bonsai_workflows import workflow_path

p = workflow_path("run-flir-flycap-1cam")
print(p)  # absolute path inside the installed package

This is what BonsaiCameraRunner calls internally.
